verses.1: In Allah’s name, the Beneficent, the Merciful.
verses.2: All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
verses.4: Master of the Day of Judgment.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that people commonly begin works in the names of honoured persons in hope of success, blessing, or lasting remembrance. God begins His speech with His own name so that its teachings are marked by it, and teaches people to begin all speech and action for God and in association with His names and attributes. What is not for God perishes, is vain, and is nullified; what is done in His name endures, receiving a share of eternity in proportion to its relation to Him. A universally accepted tradition of the Prophet accordingly says that every important affair not begun with God’s name remains incomplete; al-abtar, rendered incomplete, is that whose end has been cut off.

The preposition bi, in this setting, is connected to the implied words, I begin. Since the Qur’an was sent for the guidance of mankind, its full sense at the beginning of the Book is that total guidance begins in the name of God: the One to whom servants return, the Beneficent whose all-encompassing mercy supplies believers and unbelievers alike with what their life and existence require, and the Merciful whose special mercy gives believers happiness in the hereafter and nearness to their Lord.

God’s own designation of distinct chapters shows, in the commentary’s view, that every sūrah is a complete structural and semantic unit with its own aim. Thus, the formula at the beginning of each chapter relates to that chapter’s particular theme. The theme of the Opening appears to be God’s praise, the servant’s pledge to worship and seek help from Him alone, and the prayer for guidance. God utters this speech on behalf of His servant in order to teach gratitude and servitude. Here the servant’s central act is the pledge of servitude, so the sense is: in Thy name I begin my pledge of servitude to Thee. Although some take the implied verb to be I seek help, the commentary finds I begin more fitting, because the chapter expressly asks for help later.

Al-ism, name, in plain Arabic is the word by which an individual is spoken of or addressed, and is distinct from the named thing, whether its derivation is taken from al-simah, an identifying mark, or al-sumuww, eminence. The commentary rejects imposing on ordinary language the scholastic analysis in which an attribute such as Knowledge is a substantive divine name and the word the Knower becomes a name of that name. Ancient disputes over whether name and named are identical are therefore unnecessary: in ordinary usage they are plainly two things.

Allāh was originally al-Ilāh, with a middle letter omitted through frequent use. It may derive from worship or from bewilderment, making al-Ilāh the One worshiped or the One before whom minds are bewildered. It had become God’s proper name before the Qur’an. Other divine names can qualify Allāh, and Allāh can be the subject of verbs derived from them, but it is not used as an adjective for another name and no verb is derived from it to describe another name; this establishes its status as the proper name. Although God’s being the God of all things entails every perfection and so the name may point to all perfect attributes, the commentary maintains that it is properly a name, not a definition apart from its connection with worship or bewilderment.

Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm derive from al-raḥmah, mercy. Mercy begins as the response to another’s deficiency that moves one to supply what is needed; when attributed to God, it means bestowal that fulfils need. Al-Raḥmān has an intensive form and denotes the all-encompassing mercy given to believers and unbelievers alike. Al-Raḥīm has the form of a perpetual, inseparable attribute and is especially suited to the lasting, inexhaustible mercy bestowed on believers in the hereafter. Thus the Beneficent’s mercy is general, while the Merciful’s is reserved for believers.

Al-ḥamd differs from al-madḥ in that it praises a good acquired through the recipient’s own intention, whereas al-madḥ may praise a quality not acquired by will, such as a pearl’s lustre. Whether al in al-ḥamd denotes the whole kind of praise or every individual praise, the result is that all praise belongs to God. Everything is created by God, and everything He creates is good and beautiful; He creates by His own knowledge, power, and will, not under compulsion. His names are also wholly good, and every good and beauty proceeds from Him. Therefore, every praise uttered for a good deed in reality returns to God.

The chapter’s declaration, Thee do we worship, shows that it is revealed on man’s behalf, teaching him praise, allegiance, and humility. Yet praise is an attribution, while God transcends what servants attribute to Him. The Qur’an, as read here, directly attributes praise only to God, His purified prophets, and the people of Paradise; other creatures glorify Him with praise. Their glorification precedes praise because none but God comprehends the perfection of His acts, names, and attributes. Direct praise without first declaring His transcendence would imply enclosing Him within finite comprehension. God treats the praise of purified servants as though He Himself had uttered it because they are free from sin and defect. Proper servitude thus requires the servant to praise God in the words God has chosen for Himself. The commentary invokes a universally accepted tradition of the Prophet: no one can enumerate God’s praise, and He is as He has praised Himself. The formula all praise is due to God is therefore divine training without which the servant would not know how to praise Him.

Al-Rabb is the Master who owns and manages the affairs of what belongs to Him. Conventional social ownership is an imagined relation that permits disposal of a thing, but it is patterned upon real ownership: a person’s limbs and faculties exist through him, have no independent subsistence, and are subject to his use. God’s ownership is real, not conventional. Created things depend upon Him both for existence and for every affair connected with existence; consequently, He alone is the Lord who owns and manages everything.

Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of al-ʿālam, literally that by which something is known. It can denote the universe as a whole, a species or genus, or a group within a species. In this context, which proceeds through divine names to the Day of Judgment, the last sense is more appropriate: the worlds are the various groups of human beings and jinn, for judgment concerns mankind alone or together with the jinn.

Mālik derives from al-milk, possession, while the alternative recitation al-malik, king, derives from al-mulk, kingdom. A king has authority to administer a people but does not thereby own them or their land. God is both Master and King, and both readings are correct with respect to divine authority. Linguistically, however, king is more usual when authority is related to a time or day, and God elsewhere speaks of the kingdom of that Day. From a philosophical standpoint, every effect and all its qualities depend on their cause, and every perfection is a shadow of its cause. Since God is the Cause of all causes, perfect and independent goodness belongs only to Him; praise and thanks ultimately belong to the cause that brings perfection into being, and therefore all praise belongs to God.

Al-ʿabd means an owned human slave, and in an abstract sense may apply to other intellectual beings; modern usage often renders it servant. Al-ʿibādah, serving, worshiping, or obeying, derives from it and varies in application with its context. Al-Jawharī calls al-khuḍūʿ, submission, the basis of al-ʿubūdiyyah. The commentary first distinguishes submission as a concomitant rather than the meaning itself by noting the different constructions of al-khuḍūʿ and al-ʿibādah, but judges this grammatical argument inconclusive: synonymous terms need not take the same preposition, as al-mawlā and al-awlā illustrate.

In worshiping God, the servant stands before his Lord as a slave before a master. Worship is thus incompatible with arrogance, but not inherently with polytheism, since a slave could be jointly owned by several masters. This explains why arrogance toward worship is treated as impossible alongside actual worship, while associating another in worship is prohibited as a real possibility.

Human mastership extends only to limited matters controlled by the master. God’s mastership, by contrast, is absolute, unrestricted, and unshared; His creatures’ servitude is correspondingly absolute and undivided. He may do what He wills with and concerning them. The advance placement of Thee before do we worship, together with worship’s being stated without qualification, signifies this exclusive ownership and exclusive servitude.

The universe’s true attribute is that it is created and owned by God; nothing in it should hide His ever-present reality or distract attention from Him. True worship requires both the worshiped One and the worshiper to be present. The shift from third-person language to Thee do we worship therefore addresses God as present before the worshiper. The worshiper too must be present with body and soul, for otherwise worship is a lifeless form. He must not turn attention to anything besides God, openly as idolaters do or secretly through distraction, nor worship for entry into the Garden or escape from hell. Such diversions are forms of polytheism.

Worship is genuine only with pure intention, which the commentary calls the worshiper’s presence. Attention must not rest on another besides God, the purpose must not be some hope or fear other than God, and the worshiper must not be occupied with himself, since this would be egotism and arrogance opposed to servitude. The plural we perhaps removes the worshiper’s individual self-importance by placing him among a multitude, thereby producing humility.

Finally, saying that worship is our act might suggest independence in existence, power, or will, although the slave owns nothing. And Thee do we beseech for help removes that suggestion: the servants ascribe worship to themselves only through God’s help and are never independent of Him. The two clauses consequently express one meaning, worship with pure intention, which also explains their matching construction. The commentary notes that the following request for guidance changes the style, and that its reason is to be explained later.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains the plea, “Guide us to the straight path,” as a request that the servant’s worship, purified of every impurity, be performed on the path God has praised: the path of those upon whom He has bestowed favors. al-Ṣirāṭ, like al-ṭarīq and al-sabīl, denotes a path. All creatures travel on a prescribed course whose destination is God, yet there are distinct ways of approaching Him. Worship and prayer are the near way of believers, for God is near and answers those who call on Him; unbelievers, by contrast, are called from a far-off place. Thus, one way is near and another distant.

The commentary finds a further difference in the movement of people. Those who believe in God’s signs and are not arrogant toward His worship rise from the lower level toward the upper heights. Those upon whom divine wrath descends fall from the upper heights to lower levels. Those who adopt unbelief instead of faith have gone astray from the right way, wandering without direction. The wording of the verses accordingly distinguishes three classes: those favored by God, those afflicted by wrath, and those who have gone astray. The straight path is distinct from the latter two and belongs to believers free of arrogance toward worship, although within it there are differing degrees and branches.

Al-Mizan connects straying, polytheism, and injustice. Qur’anic passages identify going astray with abandoning faith, associating others with God, and mixing faith with injustice. Though their literal meanings differ, the three have the same practical effect and are mutually identifiable. The straight path therefore admits neither hidden deviation in belief nor outward deviation through sins or neglected good deeds. It is true monotheism in belief and action. Those who do not mix faith with injustice are secure from straying and its punishment and are promised enduring, perfect guidance; the form of the Qur’anic expression indicates a future promise of this guidance.

The people upon whom favors have been bestowed occupy a rank above even believers whose faith, obedience, and submission are complete in public and in secret. In the description of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, obedient believers are said to be “with” those favored, not to be among them. They are companions of that company rather than identical with it. Likewise, believers are included among the truthful and martyrs with their Lord in the next life. On this basis, Al-Mizan infers that the class of believers cleansed of straying continues to exist and has not ended; otherwise it would be counted among the favored rather than with them. It probably includes those given knowledge by God and raised in degrees. The favored people of the straight path possess bounties more precious than complete faith and perfect belief.

The commentary distinguishes the one straight path from the many ways of God. God attributes a single straight path to Himself, while attributing many ways to Himself, and He commonly ascribes particular ways to chosen servants. The present verse is the exception in which the straight path is related to those granted divine favors. The plural “ways” and singular “straight path” may mean either that the ways are identical with the straight path or that they ultimately meet and merge into it.

A way can contain an excellence or deficiency, whereas the straight path itself has neither defect nor deficiency. Even belief, which is a way, may coexist with a form of polytheism; the straight path cannot, because it is not the path of those who go astray. Worship and religion belong both to the various ways and to the straight path. Their relation is like that of body and soul: the body undergoes changes and may suffer effects that the soul would not accept if left to itself, while the soul remains one and does not deteriorate. Similarly, the ways remain one with the straight path but may suffer deterioration; the straight path is immune from imperfection. The ways differ in nearness, safety, purity, and degree, yet all are in, or one with, the straight path. The parable of water filling valleys according to their measure shows that hearts and minds differ in their capacity to receive divine knowledge and spiritual perfection, although they share the same divine sustenance.

The straight path governs all the ways leading to God. A particular way brings a person to God only while it remains one with the straight path, whereas the straight path reaches God without condition or failure. Al-Mizan’s lexical explanation presents al-ṣirāṭ as a clear path that holds its walkers, and al-mustaqīm as what stands firmly, controls what is attached to it, and is not subject to variation. It is therefore the path that never fails to lead its traveler to the destination: God’s unchanging course. The differing ways to God, including submission, faith, worship, purity of intention, and humility, vary in perfection, ease, and nearness to this basic reality; their opposites include unbelief, polytheism, infidelity, transgression, and sin. Spiritual knowledge also varies according to the recipient’s capacity and vision.

Because they are firmly established on the straight path, its people have complete authority to guide God’s other servants. Al-Mizan supports this with the verse declaring God, His Messenger, and those believers who keep up prayer and pay charity while bowing to be the only Master. It states that this verse was revealed about Imam ʿAlī, the Leader of the faithful, as al-mutawātir traditions say, and that he was the first to open this door in Islam.

The commentary then examines al-hidāyah. The verb may take two objects directly, as in the language of Ḥijāz, or take its second object with ilā, as in the language of other tribes. It rejects the claim that the form without ilā always means conveying someone to the destination, while the form with ilā only means showing the way. That claim appeals to the statement that the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves while God guides whom He pleases, to divine guidance expressed without a preposition, and to the Prophet’s guidance expressed with ilā. But the believer from Pharaoh’s people says, without a preposition, “I will guide you to the right course,” where the meaning can only be to show the way. The presence or absence of ilā therefore does not alter the meaning of guidance.

The statement that the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves concerns the reality or perfection of guidance, which he cannot bestow at will and which God has reserved for Himself. Guidance is showing the destination through the way and thus leading one to it. In reality God guides by creating causes that indicate the destination and carry His servants to their spiritual goal. He creates in the heart an aptitude to begin, accept, incline toward, and find repose in His remembrance. Since there are many ways to God, each has its own guidance. One person strives “in the way of God,” seeking to protect the way from dangers and obstacles; another strives “for God,” with attention fixed on God alone. The latter is praised: God guides him to the way suited to his ability and power, then continually raises him from one way to another until He attaches him exclusively to Himself.

This progressive guidance explains why a worshiper already guided to worship may still ask, “Guide us to the straight path.” God may lead a person through increasingly higher grades of the ways while preserving the straight path within them. The prayer is not an attempt to regain something already possessed, nor a request for the impossible, but a request for further guidance and ascent.

Al-Mizan also answers the objection that, since the Law brought by Muḥammad is the most perfect and comprehensive divine Law, Muslims should not ask to be guided to the path of earlier people favored by God. The superiority of a Law does not mean that every follower of it surpasses every follower of an earlier Law. An ordinary follower of Muḥammad’s Law cannot surpass Noah or Abraham merely because his Law is more perfect. Following a Law is different from attaining spiritual perfection through complete submission and being molded by that Law. A believer under an earlier Law who attained a high spiritual rank and became a mirror of divine attributes is superior to one who follows the more perfect Law without reaching that state. A lower-ranking believer may therefore ask to attain the level of a higher-ranking believer, even if the latter followed a less comprehensive Law.

The commentary rejects another exegete’s answer that all divine religions are simply one religion, Islam, with identical fundamental truths, while Islamic Law is distinguished only by its comprehensiveness, concern for public welfare, and basis in logic, admonition, and good argument. That view treats earlier people as predecessors whom Muslims should follow to spiritual perfection. Al-Mizan says its premise conflicts with sound Qur’anic exegesis, because it assumes that fundamental realities, spiritual perfections, and religious virtues have no differing grades. It would make the highest prophet and the lowest believer equal in created and natural perfection, reducing their differences to merely assumed legal positions, like those of a king and subjects. The commentary traces this outlook to materialism, which recognizes nothing but matter, except God known by logical proof. It says that its adherents were influenced either by the natural sciences and reliance on the five senses or by an appeal to commonsense that neglected meditation on the Qur’an.

Finally, Al-Mizan holds that the people of the straight path surpass others because of knowledge, not because of virtuous deeds. Perfect virtuous action can occur in lower ways and therefore cannot be the criterion of this superiority. The people of the straight path possess knowledge of the divine attributes hidden from others. The commentary defers fuller discussion of the nature and acquisition of this knowledge, but explains that true belief and knowledge are the “good words” that ascend to God, while good deeds lift them up and assist their ascent without themselves ascending.
